_comment: Combat tuning. ALL of it is TUNABLE and none of it is a mechanic. M2 exists to answer one question: is the fight worth repeating? The expected feedback is 'too slow', 'too spongy', 'the charged attack isn't worth waiting for', 'I keep missing' — every one of those has to be answerable by editing this file.
_comment_model: Combat is PILOTED, not commanded: see docs/decisions/D07-combat-is-piloted-not-commanded.md. The player takes over their pal, both fighters move inside a bounded arena, and attacks are aimed and can miss.

damage._comment: damage = power * scale * attack / (attack + defence). Bounded on purpose: a raw attack/defence ratio explodes when defence is low and produces one-shot kills that read as bugs. With scale 2, equal attack and defence deals exactly the move's power.
damage._comment_variance: Half-width of the random spread, as a fraction. 0.1 means every hit lands between 90% and 110%. Enough that two identical fights are not identical, small enough that it never decides one.

energy._comment: Charged attacks are gated on energy, and energy comes only from LANDING quick attacks. Since a quick attack can now miss, the meter is earned by connecting rather than by pressing, which is the whole spam-vs-nuke decision plus a reason to care where you are standing.

pal_movement._comment: How a creature moves while a fight is running. Faster than a walk and slower than the trainer's sprint: the fight should feel busy without turning into a foot race. TUNABLE and expected to change first if combat feels sluggish.
pal_movement._comment_impulse: How fast an attack lunge or a knockback decays, in units per second. High enough that an impulse is a punch rather than a shove.

player_quick._comment: The bread-and-butter attack. Short wind-up, short recovery, wide arc: it should be usable under pressure without feeling like a commitment.
player_quick._comment_range: Metres from the attacker's centre. Placeholder creatures are about a metre across, so this is roughly a body length of reach.
player_quick._comment_cone: Full width of the hit arc in degrees, centred on facing. 100 is DELIBERATELY forgiving: you can still miss by facing the wrong way or being out of range, so spacing and facing are real skills, but a narrow arc on a 7-inch handheld makes 'I missed' the dominant feeling of every early fight.

player_charged._comment: The commitment. Long wind-up and long recovery mean throwing it at the wrong moment is punished by the opponent closing on a rooted target; that spatial cost is what makes it a decision rather than just a better button.
player_charged._comment_cone: Tighter than the quick attack. Spending a full meter and missing should be possible, or the charged attack has no downside at all.

enemy._comment: The opponent's brain lives in scripts/combat/combat_ai.gd; these are its numbers. It closes, commits to an attack, is rooted while it recovers, then backs off and comes again. The recovery window is the player's punish opportunity and is the single most important number here.
enemy._comment_preferred: It stops closing at this distance and attacks from there. Must be under `range` or it stands just outside its own reach and whiffs forever.
enemy._comment_reposition: After recovering it backs off and circles for this long before closing again. Without it the fight is two creatures standing in each other's faces trading hits, which is exactly the static fight this model replaced.
enemy._comment_body_clearance: How far apart two creatures stand, as a multiple of their combined body radii. It FLOORS `preferred_range` rather than replacing it: the config still decides how much breathing room a fight wants, and this only refuses to let it be less than the two bodies occupy. The flat 2.1m below was written when every creature was the same capsule; with real models it is smaller than the pair, so the opponent walked to 2.1m and stopped with its head inside the other creature's flank. The blind critic found that in five of seven combat frames, once with antlers coming out of the other creature's back. Reach and reposition distance are floored to match, or a creature spaces itself to exactly where it can no longer hit anything. Raised from 1.35: `body_radius` is the GAMEPLAY collider, and pal_body fits art to it with a footprint allowance of 2.4, so a model is routinely wider than the capsule that represents it. Spacing by the collider alone still left the meshes overlapping.

arena._comment: The bounded space a fight happens in, centred on where it started. Both fighters are held inside it. Walking into the edge slides you along it; it is NOT how you flee, because ending a fight by accident while backing away would be infuriating. Run is how you flee.
arena._comment_boundary: Height and opacity of the drawn wall. It has to be visible enough to be read as a boundary and faint enough not to obscure the fight happening inside it.
arena._comment_short: Short and reasonably solid rather than tall and faint. A tall translucent drum reads as haze across the horizon; a bright band at ground level reads as an edge.
arena._comment_deploy: Where the two fighters start, measured forward from the trainer along the line they were engaged on. The trainer is never moved and never targeted.
arena._comment_boundary_alpha: Higher than it looks, because the boundary is now ADDITIVE with a vertical falloff baked into its vertex colours — brightest at the ground, gone by the top — rather than a flat translucent cylinder. The old flat version read as a hard-edged khaki band splatted onto the terrain, in the same hue family as the hills behind it.

flow._comment_engage: Metres at which the interact prompt appears. Engagement is ALWAYS an explicit button press: GAME_DESIGN.md 14 forbids proximity starting a fight with a peaceful pal.
flow._comment_guard: Seconds of player input ignored at the start of a fight. Engage and charged attack are the same physical button (X), and without this the press that opens the fight is also read as the first attack of it.

camera._comment: The fight reuses the exploration orbit camera rather than adding a second one: a piloted pal wants exactly the third-person camera M1 already tuned, re-pointed at a shorter creature. These are the overrides while a fight is running.
camera._comment_distance: Close. These are metre-tall creatures, not a 1.8m trainer: at the exploration camera's 5.2m they read as specks and the fight is unreadable.
camera._comment_height: Pivot height above the pal's feet. Above the creature rather than at its shoulder, so the camera looks slightly DOWN on the fight and the ground the opponent is standing on stays in frame.
camera._comment_fov: Narrower than exploration's 70. A wide lens this close distorts both creatures towards the edges of the frame, which is exactly where a fight with free movement puts them.
camera._comment_shoulder: Metres the lens slides sideways. Dead centre behind your own pal means your own pal covers the opponent, which is the one thing you must be able to see.
camera._comment_blend: How fast the rig eases onto the pal when a fight opens, and back onto the trainer when it ends.

wild._comment: How a wild pal behaves before it is engaged. It never initiates: GAME_DESIGN.md 14 requires proximity not to start a fight with a peaceful pal. It wanders so it does not read as scenery, and it stops and looks at you so there is a cue that it can be engaged at all.

impact._comment: The visual event of a blow landing. ALL tunable presentation; nothing here touches damage, reach or timing.
impact._comment_measured: The blind critic counted bright warm pixels at the instant of contact: 10 in `combat/05-quick-attack-lands`, 295 in `combat/06`, and 24,623 in `palworld-01` — roughly ten thousand times the visual energy for the same beat. Its reading was that the only difference between the frame before a hit and the frame of the hit was that the health bar got shorter. Turn `enabled` off to get that back.
impact._comment_charged: Bigger and warmer than a quick hit. If the expensive move looks like the free one, building energy was never worth doing.
impact._comment_size: Small and brief. The first attempt used 1.35/1.9 metre radii that expanded to nearly two and a half times that, and from the combat camera's downward angle the camera-facing ring lay across the ground like a decal five metres wide — it read as a texture bug rather than as a blow landing. An impact is a point event; if it is big enough to notice on a still it is far too big in motion.
impact._comment_contrast: Near-WHITE, not beige. The critic measured the old burst at 2.47-3.10:1 contrast against olive ground and observed that a landing hit was lower-contrast than the trainer standing still: 'a landing hit should be the highest-contrast event in the frame'. Against a mid-green world the highest-contrast thing available is white, and the warmth can come from the charged variant rather than from dulling both.
